title: How are sealed classes and records complementary in Java's pattern-matching vision?
shortTitle: How are sealed classes and records complementary in Java's pattern-matching vision?

s1_definition.profdef: A sealed type defines a closed set of permitted subtypes, which is a "sum type" — a value is exactly one of a fixed list of alternatives. A record defines an immutable, transparent "product type" — a value is a fixed bundle of named components. Together they form algebraic data types, and Java's pattern matching uses them as two halves of one design: sealed types let the compiler prove a `switch` is exhaustive (it covers every alternative), and record deconstruction patterns let you pull the components out of each alternative in one step. The two features combine so you can match on which alternative a value is and bind its data at the same time, with compile-time exhaustiveness.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed menu of exactly three transaction types: Deposit, Withdrawal, and Transfer — that closed menu is the sealed type. Each transaction type is a pre-printed form with fixed fields: a Transfer form always has "from account", "to account", and "amount" — that fixed form is the record. When a clerk processes a transaction, they first look at which form it is (sum type choice) and then immediately read the fields printed on it (product type data). The sealed menu guarantees the clerk has a handling rule for every possible form, and the record forms guarantee each form's fields are read cleanly in one glance.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealed types say "it is exactly one of these," records say "and here are its fields," and pattern matching reads both in a single exhaustive switch.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sealed type defines a closed set of permitted subtypes, which is a "sum type" — a value is exactly one of a fixed list of alternatives. A record defines an immutable, transparent "product type" — a value is a fixed bundle of named components. Together they form algebraic data types, and Java's pattern matching uses them as two halves of one design: sealed types let the compiler prove a `switch` is exhaustive (it covers every alternative), and record deconstruction patterns let you pull the components out of each alternative in one step. The two features combine so you can match on which alternative a value is and bind its data at the same time, with compile-time exhaustiveness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed menu of exactly three transaction types: Deposit, Withdrawal, and Transfer — that closed menu is the sealed type. Each transaction type is a pre-printed form with fixed fields: a Transfer form always has "from account", "to account", and "amount" — that fixed form is the record. When a clerk processes a transaction, they first look at which form it is (sum type choice) and then immediately read the fields printed on it (product type data). The sealed menu guarantees the clerk has a handling rule for every possible form, and the record forms guarantee each form's fields are read cleanly in one glance.

**One line to remember:** Sealed types say "it is exactly one of these," records say "and here are its fields," and pattern matching reads both in a single exhaustive switch.

sections.s2_technical:
A sealed hierarchy is a sum type: `sealed interface Txn permits Deposit, Withdrawal, Transfer`. A record is a product type: `record Transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) implements Txn`. The compiler knows the sealed set is closed, so a `switch` over `Txn` that handles `Deposit`, `Withdrawal`, and `Transfer` needs no `default` branch. If someone later adds a fourth permitted type, every switch that was exhaustive now fails to compile, pointing you at the exact places to update. This is the single most valuable interaction: closed sets plus exhaustive switch turns "forgot a case" from a runtime bug into a compile error.

Records add two superpowers to that switch. First, record patterns let you deconstruct directly in a case: `case Transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) -> ...` binds the three components without calling accessors. For example you can write `case Transfer(var from, var to, var amount) -> log.info(() -> "Transfer " + amount + " " + from + "→" + to)`. Second, records are transparent and immutable, so the compiler knows their canonical components and can even support nested deconstruction such as `case Transfer(Account(var id, var bal), var to, var amount) -> ...` when `from` is itself a record.

The deeper vision is that Java is moving pattern matching from a niche feature toward a primary way to model and process data. Sealed types model the shape of the data domain (the alternatives), records model the content of each alternative (the fields), and pattern matching in `switch` and `instanceof` consumes both. A senior nuance: records being implicitly final fits sealed hierarchies perfectly, because permitted subtypes must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, and a record satisfies the `final` requirement automatically. Another nuance: guarded patterns (`case Transfer t when t.amount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0`) layer business conditions on top of structural matching, still keeping exhaustiveness for the unguarded cases.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes a stream of transactions. Every transaction is exactly one of a small, fixed set of kinds, and the bank must handle every kind or the audit fails. This is exactly how a sealed interface works — it closes the set of transaction kinds so the compiler can force us to handle all of them.

Problem 2 — For each kind, the clerk needs to read specific fields immediately: a Transfer needs from, to, and amount; a Deposit needs an account and amount. Writing getter calls everywhere is noisy and error-prone. This is exactly how records plus record patterns work — each kind is a tidy immutable bundle, and deconstruction reads its fields in the same line where we match the kind.

The demo defines a sealed interface `Txn` with three record implementors, processes Rajesh's and Priya's transactions through one exhaustive `switch` that uses record deconstruction, and shows that adding a new kind would break compilation until handled. Classes and steps: `Txn` (sealed interface), `Deposit`, `Withdrawal`, `Transfer` (records), `Account` (record for nested deconstruction), `TxnProcessor` (the exhaustive switch), and `BankDemo` (main).

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Deposit of Rs.20,000 into Priya (CUR3001), a Withdrawal of Rs.5,000 from Rajesh (SAV2001), and a Transfer of Rs.50,000 from Rajesh to Priya.

Step 1 — Each transaction is created as a specific record implementing the sealed `Txn` interface. The data is immutable the moment it is constructed.

Step 2 — `describe` runs a `switch` over the closed `Txn` set. The compiler already verified at compile time that `Deposit`, `Withdrawal`, and `Transfer` are the only possibilities, so the switch is exhaustive without a default.

Step 3 — For the Deposit, the record pattern `Deposit(Account(var id, var bal), var amount)` deconstructs the deposit and, nested inside it, the `Account`, binding `id`, `bal`, and `amount` in one move. The output names Priya's account and amount.

Step 4 — For the Transfer, the guarded case checks the amount against Rs.100,000 first. The Rs.50,000 transfer does not exceed the limit, so it falls through to the plain Transfer case and is described as a normal transfer from SAV2001 to CUR3001.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Result: DEPOSIT Rs.20000 into CUR3001 (old bal Rs.250000)
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Result: WITHDRAW Rs.5000 from SAV2001 (old bal Rs.1000000)
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Result: TRANSFER Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: List<Txn> [ Deposit, Withdrawal, Transfer ]
    │
    ▼
  TxnProcessor.describe(txn)  — switch over SEALED set (exhaustive, no default)
    │
    ├─ case Deposit(Account(id,bal), amt)      ───→ "DEPOSIT ..."   (record deconstruct + nested)
    ├─ case Withdrawal(Account(id,bal), amt)   ───→ "WITHDRAW ..."
    ├─ case Transfer(from,to,amt) when amt>1L  ───→ "HIGH-VALUE ..." (guarded)
    └─ case Transfer(from,to,amt)              ───→ "TRANSFER ..."
    │
    ▼
  Add a 4th permitted kind later  →  EVERY exhaustive switch FAILS to compile
                                     (compiler points to each site to fix)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealed classes and records are the two halves of algebraic data types in Java, and pattern matching is what brings them together. A sealed type is a sum type: it says a value is exactly one of a fixed, closed set of alternatives. A record is a product type: it says a value is an immutable bundle of named components. Because a sealed hierarchy is closed, the compiler can prove that a switch over it is exhaustive and reject it if I miss a case, and because records are transparent, I can deconstruct their components directly inside each case with a record pattern.

In my banking system at National Bank of India I modeled transactions as a sealed interface called Txn that permits three records: Deposit, Withdrawal, and Transfer. When I process Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, a single switch handles every kind with no default branch, and inside each case I use record deconstruction to read the account and amount in one line. For transfers I even nest the deconstruction to pull the account id and balance out of the embedded Account record, and I layer a guarded case so that any transfer above one hundred thousand rupees is flagged as high value needing approval, while smaller transfers fall through to the normal case.

The real payoff is safety and clarity together. If the bank later introduces a fourth transaction kind, say a standing instruction, I add it to the permits list, and immediately every exhaustive switch across the codebase fails to compile until I handle the new kind. That turns "we forgot to handle a case" from a production incident into a compile error the moment I build. At the same time, record patterns keep the processing code clean because I never write a chain of getter calls; I read the structure declaratively.

So in an interview I summarize it like this: sealed types describe which alternatives exist, records describe the fields inside each alternative, and pattern matching consumes both at once, giving me compiler-checked exhaustiveness plus clean data deconstruction. That combination is exactly why Java's modern pattern-matching design treats sealed classes and records as complementary rather than separate features.
